items.question: A pharmacy chain's in-store systems reach a cloud-hosted Claude service over a private circuit and a private service endpoint. A network review finds that traffic from a subset of stores is leaving through the corporate internet proxy instead, even though the private path is up and the routes are correct. What is the most likely cause and the right remediation?

options.A: The private circuit is saturated at those sites and traffic is overflowing to the internet path; increase circuit bandwidth and reprioritise the traffic class.
options.B: The corporate proxy has the service's public addresses in its allowlist; remove those entries so the proxy rejects the traffic from those stores.
options.C: TLS validation fails against the private endpoint, so clients retry over the proxy; install the endpoint's certificate chain in the store systems' trust stores.
options.D: Those sites' resolvers still return the service's public address; make private DNS authoritative for that hostname everywhere and add an egress deny.

items.question: A payroll SaaS serves customers in the EU, the UK and Australia. Each contract commits that the customer's employee data is processed and stored in that customer's own region. The product currently runs one deployment with one Claude integration, and a `region` column on the tenant table. Users frequently travel and log in from anywhere. What architecture meets the commitments?

options.A: Keep the single deployment and enforce the commitment with row-level filtering on the tenant's region column plus a separate encryption key held per region.
options.B: Keep one deployment for processing but replicate each tenant's stored records into a regional database, so storage is resident while inference stays centralised.
options.C: Deploy an independent data plane per residency zone and route each request to the zone named by the tenant's residency attribute, keeping control metadata global.
options.D: Deploy per-region stacks and route each request to the region geographically closest to the user, since that minimises latency and keeps data near where it is used.

items.question: A mining group has a large multi-year committed spend agreement with one public cloud and mature cost allocation built on that cloud's resource tagging, feeding monthly showback by cost centre. A new Claude workload is being planned; the engineering team has no technical preference between routes. What should most influence the recommendation, and what does it imply?

options.A: Nothing commercial should drive it; pick the first-party API for the most direct relationship with the model provider and negotiate a separate agreement for it.
options.B: Model spend will be small next to the group's infrastructure bill, so the decision should be deferred until three months of usage data exists.
options.C: Consumption should draw down the existing cloud commitment and inherit the established tagging and showback model, pointing at that cloud's managed service.
options.D: Build a chargeback service that ingests the provider's usage export and maps it to cost centres, which makes the route choice commercially neutral.

items.question: Why do teams provision a second concurrently valid credential for a service before rotating the one currently in use?

options.A: It provides a fallback if the provider rejects the primary credential during an incident, so the service can immediately retry the call with the other.
options.B: It makes rotation a rolling operation: the new credential is deployed and verified while the old one is still accepted, and only then is the old one revoked.
options.C: It doubles the throughput available to the service, since request quota is generally allocated per credential rather than per account.
options.D: It allows two teams to share the same service integration without either team seeing the credential value the other one holds.

items.question: A biotechnology company's research group runs Claude experiments from personal laptops and a shared notebook server. An audit finds credentials pasted into notebook cells, present in shell history, and committed to the internal git server. Which TWO controls prevent a raw credential from being present in a researcher's environment or repository in the first place? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Enable secret scanning on the git server as a pre-receive check, so a push containing a credential is rejected rather than reported afterwards.
options.B: Run a nightly scan of the notebook server's filesystem that alerts the platform team when a string resembling a credential is found.
options.C: Provide a shared client library and notebook kernel that obtain a short-lived token from the platform's identity service at session start.
options.D: Issue one credential per researcher so that any leak can be attributed to an individual and revoked without disrupting the rest of the group.
options.E: Rotate the shared research credential monthly and circulate the new value on the research group's private chat channel each cycle.

items.question: A ride-hailing company's gateway tracks per-team monthly model budgets and alerts on breach. One team's runaway backfill consumed most of the company's monthly model spend in six hours overnight; the alert fired at 03:00 and nobody acted until morning. The CFO wants hard caps. The platform team is worried, because a hard cap could cut off the driver-safety escalation flow that shares the same provider account. What enforcement design should the platform team propose?

options.A: Enforce per-team hard caps and a spend-rate circuit breaker, reserve a floor for the safety-critical class, and require break-glass to raise any cap.
options.B: Enforce per-request cost limits so that no individual call can be unexpectedly expensive, keeping the monthly team budgets advisory as they are today.
options.C: Apply one company-wide hard cap set slightly above the historical monthly peak spend, so no single team's backfill can exhaust the account.
options.D: Keep alert-only enforcement but route budget alerts to a 24-hour on-call rota with an explicit response runbook and a 15-minute acknowledgement target.

items.question: A platform team is choosing between a shared central gateway and a per-service sidecar proxy for outbound model traffic. Which statement correctly characterises the trade-off?

options.A: A sidecar cannot hold credentials or enforce policy, so it is only useful for collecting metrics; enforcement always requires a central component in the path.
options.B: Sidecars remove the need to define policy centrally, because each service team owns and enforces the rules appropriate to its own workload.
options.C: The gateway concentrates credentials, policy and observability in one operated component but sits in every request path; the sidecar trades that for fleet-wide rollouts.
options.D: A central gateway is unsuitable for latency-sensitive workloads, because the additional in-region hop dominates end-to-end response time for short prompts.

items.question: An enterprise requires that model traffic originating in its own data centre reach a cloud-hosted Claude service without traversing the public internet. Which combination is required?

options.A: Mutual TLS between the on-premises client and the service endpoint, with the client certificate issued by the enterprise's own internal certificate authority and pinned.
options.B: A private circuit between the data centre and the cloud, a private service endpoint in the virtual network, and DNS returning that private address on-premises.
options.C: A site-to-site VPN across the public internet using strong ciphers and perfect forward secrecy, plus certificate pinning on every on-premises client.
options.D: A static egress address registered on the provider's source allowlist, with all other outbound traffic from the data centre denied by policy.

items.question: A port authority receives a nightly fixed-width file of roughly 90,000 cargo movements over SFTP from a terminal-operating system that cannot be modified. An acknowledgement file must be returned by 05:00. The business wants Claude to normalise free-text cargo descriptions. The inbound file occasionally arrives late, and occasionally the transfer is still in progress when the pipeline starts reading. What design should the team adopt?

options.A: Require the terminal-operating system to publish movements to an API instead, removing the nightly file transfer and its timing problems entirely.
options.B: Gate processing on the sender's completion marker, enrich asynchronously keyed on file digest plus row identifier, and pass rows through unnormalised if 05:00 is reached.
options.C: Begin reading rows as soon as the file appears so enrichment overlaps the transfer, and re-read the tail if the final row count looks short.
options.D: Enrich each row synchronously inside the file reader so the acknowledgement file can be written as soon as the last of the 90,000 rows is read.

items.question: A benefits agency is publishing an asynchronous Claude-backed eligibility-explanation API to about 30 internal consuming teams. Which THREE elements must the job status resource expose for consumers to be able to behave correctly? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The job's current position in the processing queue, so each consuming team can display an accurate estimated wait to its own users.
options.B: A machine-readable failure classification separating retryable conditions from permanent ones, so consumers do not resubmit work that can never succeed.
options.C: An explicit distinction between terminal and non-terminal states, so a consumer knows when to stop polling and can tell 'still working' from 'finished'.
options.D: The full prompt sent to the model for that job, so each consuming team can audit exactly what was asked on its claimants' behalf.
options.E: A documented retention period for the job record and its result, so consumers know how long a handle stays resolvable and what a missing handle means.

items.question: A rail operator's disruption service makes a direct HTTP call to a Claude-based passenger-message generator whenever a disruption is declared. Three more teams now want the same trigger: crew notification, social-post drafting, and station display copy. The disruption service team is being asked to add three more outbound calls, and is resisting because it is already paged when the message generator is slow. What should the architect propose?

options.A: Add the three calls to the disruption service but issue them from a background thread pool so the declaring transaction is never delayed by them.
options.B: Publish the disruption event once to a topic and let each consumer subscribe with its own queue, retry policy and failure isolation.
options.C: Have each of the four consumers poll the disruption service's API every thirty seconds for disruptions declared since the previous poll.
options.D: Have the passenger-message generator call the three new consumers once it has finished, keeping the disruption service's integration surface unchanged.

items.question: A food-delivery company runs order events through a stream into enrichment workers that call Claude, then into a downstream scoring service. During a Friday surge the worker pool autoscaled on CPU utilisation, which stayed low because workers spend most of their time awaiting model responses. The pool grew rapidly, model rejections climbed, retries multiplied, and the scoring service was overwhelmed. What is the correct remediation?

options.A: Scale the worker pool on in-flight model concurrency and consumer lag, with a hard ceiling on total concurrency set from the account's sustainable capacity.
options.B: Scale the downstream scoring service in proportion to the worker pool so it can absorb whatever throughput the enrichment workers produce.
options.C: Increase the number of stream partitions so more enrichment workers can process order events in parallel and the Friday surge drains faster.
options.D: Raise the CPU utilisation target on the worker autoscaler so that it adds replicas far less aggressively during a Friday surge.

items.question: A travel-booking platform delivers 'itinerary summary ready' webhooks to corporate travel partners. One partner's endpoint has returned server errors for six hours; about 14,000 deliveries for that partner are queued and retrying every thirty seconds. Those retries are now consuming most of the shared delivery worker pool, and deliveries to healthy partners are running hours late. What should the on-call engineer do next?

options.A: Move the failing partner's deliveries onto their own bounded queue behind a circuit breaker with a long backoff and a periodic probe.
options.B: Disable webhook delivery for that partner entirely and notify their operations contact to pull the missed itinerary summaries manually.
options.C: Discard queued deliveries for the failing partner that are older than an hour, since the itinerary data will be stale by the time the endpoint returns.
options.D: Scale the delivery worker pool up sharply so there is enough capacity for both the failing partner's retries and the healthy partners.

items.question: A hospital group's clinician portal cannot manage background jobs: its front-end framework can only issue a request and render a response. The internal Claude pipeline behind the requested feature is queue-based, with p50 of 2 seconds and p95 of 12 seconds, and the portal's HTTP client times out at 15 seconds. What should the platform team expose?

options.A: The existing asynchronous contract, with guidance that the portal team implement polling, since that is the correct client-side pattern for long work.
options.B: A synchronous endpoint that bypasses the pipeline and calls the model directly, so the queue's latency variability is removed from the portal's path.
options.C: A synchronous endpoint that submits to the pipeline and blocks until the job completes, however long the queue and the model take.
options.D: A facade that submits to the pipeline, waits up to a deadline inside the portal's timeout, and returns either the result or a resolvable handle.

items.question: A professional-services firm has run Claude on the first-party API for eighteen months. A new group CIO mandates that third-party AI services be consumed through the group's primary cloud. Which TWO items represent genuine migration work the plan must budget for? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Re-running the firm's evaluation suite against the new route and re-establishing pinned model identifiers, which differ between hosting routes.
options.B: Rebuilding the retrieval index, because embeddings produced under one hosting route cannot be used with another and would all need regenerating.
options.C: Renegotiating the firm's retention and residency position from scratch, because commitments of that kind are unavailable on cloud-hosted routes.
options.D: Rewriting the firm's entire prompt library, because prompt syntax and system-message structure differ between the two hosting routes.
options.E: Rebuilding the identity and credential path, since authentication moves from a provider key to the cloud's identity model, along with the network route.

items.question: A hospital group's Claude assistant answers clinicians' questions over patient records. Its backend authenticates to the records system with one service account holding broad read access, retrieves records, and filters them in application code according to the signed-in clinician's care-team membership. A risk review flags the design. What should change?

options.A: Exchange the clinician's authenticated session for a delegated token and call the records system on their behalf, so it applies its own authorisation.
options.B: Keep the current retrieval and add an output check that removes any record the signed-in clinician is not entitled to see before the response is returned.
options.C: Keep the service account but create one per clinical department, so the breadth of standing read access is reduced to that department's records.
options.D: Include the clinician's role and care-team membership in the prompt and instruct the model to withhold any records outside their entitlement.

items.question: A pension administrator's gateway writes every model request and response body to an audit store, supporting a regulator-facing commitment that any interaction can be reproduced for seven years. A routine review finds that for the past three weeks any body exceeding a configured size limit was silently dropped, with only metadata retained. About 12% of interactions are affected. What should the architect do next?

options.A: Reconstruct the missing records by replaying the affected requests against the model and storing the resulting outputs as the audit record for those interactions.
options.B: Migrate the audit store to object storage with no practical size limit, and treat the historical gap as immaterial given that 88% of interactions were captured.
options.C: Raise the configured size limit generously, add an alert for any future occurrence, and close the finding as remediated in the control register.
options.D: Change the gateway to reject rather than serve any interaction whose audit record cannot be written in full, and raise the gap as a reportable control failure.

items.question: A six-person engineering team at a national charity runs one Claude-backed feature that drafts donor correspondence. There is one application, one environment and one credential. A consulting architect recommends they build a central gateway with quota enforcement, provider routing and an audit store. What should the team do?

options.A: Build the gateway now, because retrofitting one after the donor-correspondence feature is live would mean re-plumbing a running production integration.
options.B: Self-host an open-source gateway cluster so quota enforcement, routing and audit exist without the charity building any of it in-house.
options.C: Do neither, since with one application, one environment and one credential there is nothing that a gateway or its controls would add here.
options.D: Keep the single application, resolve the credential at runtime, add request and response logging with cost visibility, and revisit a gateway later.

items.question: An engineering consultancy queues design-review requests for Claude analysis. Each request carries a specification document of around 30 MB plus client-confidential drawings, far above the broker's message size limit, so the team currently base64-encodes and splits documents across many messages with a reassembly step. Separately, the platform operations team can read message bodies on the broker but is not permitted to see client documents. What should the design change to?

options.A: Keep the chunking scheme but encrypt each chunk with a key held in the delivery team's vault that the operations team cannot access.
options.B: Raise the broker's maximum message size, or move to a broker that supports large messages, so the chunking and reassembly step is no longer needed.
options.C: Write the payload to an access-controlled object store and place only a reference, a content digest and a short-lived access grant on the queue for the worker.
options.D: Keep the chunking scheme but compress each document first and add a reassembly checksum so that partial sets are detected before analysis.

items.question: A defence electronics manufacturer's security authority states that a proposed AI capability must run fully air-gapped, with no network dependency on an external party. A programme manager has already committed the capability to a customer milestone. As the architect, what is the right course of action?

options.A: Take the requirement back to the security authority and decompose it into the specific controls it protects, since no hosted route can satisfy a literal air-gap.
options.B: Place a caching layer inside the enclave that serves previously seen responses, so the majority of requests never cross the enclave boundary during normal operation.
options.C: Commit now to running a self-hosted model inside the enclave on the programme's own hardware, since only that satisfies the wording as written.
options.D: Provision a private circuit and private endpoint and describe the resulting design as air-gapped in the security accreditation documentation.

items.question: A national broadcaster governs model access centrally: one platform cloud account holds the approved configuration, the private endpoints and the audit logging. Twelve product accounts need to call the model. Which TWO arrangements are sound? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Each product account provisions its own direct model access, and the platform account reconciles usage exports afterwards to confirm compliance.
options.B: Each product workload assumes a role in the platform account scoped to model invocation, with a trust policy naming the product roles permitted to assume it.
options.C: The platform account exposes its gateway on a private endpoint that product accounts connect to, keeping the path inside private address space.
options.D: The platform account issues each product team a long-lived credential, which the team stores in its own account's secret manager and rotates on its own schedule.
options.E: The platform account's role is granted permission to assume roles in each of the twelve product accounts so it can invoke the model on their behalf.

items.question: A chemical manufacturer routes all outbound traffic through a forward proxy that performs TLS inspection using a corporate certificate authority; the security standard permits no inspection bypasses. A new Claude integration fails at connection time with certificate validation errors, and a developer proposes disabling certificate verification in the SDK. What should the architect direct instead?

options.A: Install the corporate authority in the runtime's trust store so validation succeeds, and assess the proxy's logging and retention now that it sees plaintext.
options.B: Configure the application to connect over plain HTTP to the proxy and let the proxy establish TLS onward, avoiding all certificate handling in the application.
options.C: Disable verification for this destination only, since the corporate proxy already inspects and protects every connection leaving the estate.
options.D: Pin the model provider's certificate in the application so the connection is validated against a known-good certificate rather than the proxy's.

items.question: An insurance broker is moving a Claude-backed policy-comparison service from the first-party API to a cloud-hosted route. The service handles about two million calls a month, downtime is not acceptable, and the head of product's main worry is that a quality or latency regression would go unnoticed for weeks. All traffic already flows through the broker's gateway. What cutover approach should the architect propose?

options.A: Cut over in the pre-production environment first and promote to production once the full regression and evaluation suite passes against the new route.
options.B: Mirror a sample of production traffic to the new route without serving its output, compare results and latency, then shift traffic by percentage with automatic rollback.
options.C: Send every request to both routes and serve whichever response returns first, retiring the slower route once a clear winner emerges from the data.
options.D: Perform a single cutover during a low-traffic weekend window, with a documented rollback to the previous route if problems are reported afterwards.

items.question: An interaction begins as a synchronous API call, is placed on a queue, is processed by a model worker, and is delivered onward by a webhook. What does propagating one correlation identifier through every hop provide?

options.A: Ordering, since every component can sort work into identifier sequence when messages arrive out of order after the queue hop.
options.B: Deduplication, since a repeated identifier lets each component recognise and discard any work it has already performed for that interaction.
options.C: The ability to reconstruct one logical interaction end to end across components that never share a call stack, so an operator can trace a request.
options.D: Authentication continuity, since downstream components can trust a request that carries an identifier issued by the authenticated entry point of the chain.

items.question: A car-rental group is writing the disaster-recovery design for its Claude-based damage-assessment feature, with a 15-minute recovery point objective and a one-hour recovery time objective. Which THREE items must the design cover? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The job and outbox tables, because in-flight submissions and unpublished events cannot be reconstructed from any other source after a regional loss.
options.B: A warm standby capacity commitment from the model provider, contractually guaranteed to the group's one-hour recovery time objective and exercised quarterly.
options.C: The credential, network and configuration path in the recovery region — identity, private endpoint and model identifier mapping — proven by an exercise.
options.D: The prompt template library, replicated synchronously to the recovery region because it cannot be rebuilt after a regional loss.
options.E: The audit store of requests and responses, because it is the only record of what was actually sent and returned and cannot be regenerated.

items.question: A market-research agency exposes an asynchronous Claude-backed transcript-analysis API to forty client organisations. Each client received a static API key by email at onboarding; almost none have ever rotated one, and two keys have turned up in client-side code. What should the agency move to?

options.A: Add per-client source-address allowlisting so a leaked key is unusable from anywhere except the client's registered corporate network ranges.
options.B: Keep the static keys but mandate 90-day rotation in the client agreement and remind each client by email when a key is due to age out.
options.C: Keep the shared secret but require clients to sign each request with an HMAC over the body and a timestamp rather than presenting the key as a bearer token.
options.D: Issue per-client credentials through a standard client-credentials flow with short-lived scoped tokens, self-service rotation and a deprecation date for the static keys.

items.question: A credit union receives signed webhooks from its core banking vendor and rejects any delivery whose signed timestamp falls outside a 30-second freshness window. Since a data-centre migration, about 4% of deliveries are rejected as stale; the vendor's retries eventually succeed, so nothing is lost but processing is delayed. An engineer finds that the receiving hosts' clocks drift by as much as 45 seconds from a reliable reference. What should be done next?

options.A: Widen the freshness window to five minutes so that normal clock drift on the receiving hosts no longer causes rejections.
options.B: Stop checking the timestamp and rely on the signature alone, which already proves the delivery came from the core banking vendor.
options.C: Restore reliable time synchronisation on the receiving hosts and alert on clock offset, leaving the window as it is.
options.D: Ask the vendor to include a monotonic sequence number so the receiver can accept out-of-window deliveries it has not already seen.

items.question: An online betting operator generates settlement explanations from queued events. The consumer deduplicates on an idempotency key held in an in-memory cache with a one-hour time-to-live. The upstream broker escalates its retry backoff and can redeliver as late as 24 hours after the first attempt, which happens after long partner outages. Duplicate settlement explanations have appeared following two such outages. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Switch the cache from time-based expiry to least-recently-used eviction so that keys survive for as long as the cache's capacity allows.
options.B: Increase the cache's memory allocation so that idempotency keys are not evicted under load during the busiest settlement periods.
options.C: Shorten the broker's maximum retry horizon to one hour so a redelivery can never arrive after the deduplication window has closed.
options.D: Move the deduplication key to durable storage outliving the maximum redelivery horizon, and enforce uniqueness on the terminal database write.

items.question: A semiconductor fab's yield-analysis service runs its full test suite on every pull request, around 120 a week, and every run makes live Claude calls. Pipelines are slow, intermittently fail on transient provider errors, cost more than the team expected, and require a production-capable credential to be available to CI. What should the team adopt?

options.A: Keep the live calls but cache responses keyed on a hash of the request, so repeated test runs mostly hit the cache instead of the provider.
options.B: Point continuous integration at the cheapest model tier so the cost of live calls across 120 pull requests a week becomes acceptable to the team.
options.C: Use a recorded stub of the provider by default so pipelines are deterministic and need no credential, plus a scheduled suite against the real provider.
options.D: Mock the provider in unit tests only, and keep the integration tests calling the live provider so real behaviour is always exercised on every pull request.

items.question: Under which condition should a partner integration deliver results by polling rather than by webhook?

options.A: When the producer wants to avoid managing per-consumer delivery secrets, since a polling consumer needs no shared credential of its own.
options.B: When the consumer cannot expose a reachable, authenticated inbound endpoint, so a cursor-based polling contract is the only option.
options.C: When event volume is very high, because polling scales better than maintaining a delivery queue and retry schedule for each consumer.
options.D: When the consumer requires the lowest achievable notification latency, since a poll returns immediately whereas a webhook must be queued for delivery.

items.question: A recruitment platform serves all tenants from one provider account. An enterprise tenant launched a bulk CV-screening job that consumed most of the available concurrency for forty minutes. During that period p95 latency for interactive candidate searches rose from 1.5 to 9 seconds — for every tenant, including recruiters at the tenant running the bulk job. Contracts commit to an interactive p95. What should the platform team implement?

options.A: Provision a separate provider account per enterprise tenant, so tenants are physically isolated from one another's concurrency consumption.
options.B: Apply a uniform per-tenant concurrency cap, sized so that no single tenant can consume more than its equal share of the account's total concurrency budget.
options.C: Place all requests in a single queue processed strictly first-in-first-out, so every tenant and every request is treated identically.
options.D: Separate workload classes: a reserved lane with admission control for interactive traffic, and a lower-ceilinged lane for bulk work on spare capacity.

items.question: A water utility extracts customer-complaint free text from a mainframe file for Claude summarisation. The file is fixed-width, defined by a COBOL copybook, encoded in EBCDIC, and includes packed-decimal numeric fields. The first production run produces garbled summaries containing numbers that do not appear anywhere in the source data. Which TWO explanations are the likely causes? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The file was transferred in binary mode and the text fields were never transcoded from EBCDIC, so the model received bytes read as the wrong character set.
options.B: Packed-decimal fields were read as character data, so numeric values reached the prompt as unprintable bytes that the model rendered as plausible figures.
options.C: Sampling settings were left at their provider defaults, producing wording that varies across successive runs of the same complaint extract.
options.D: The copybook defines fixed-width records with no delimiters, so the model cannot parse the extract into named fields without separators being inserted first.
options.E: The extract exceeded the model's context window, so the middle of each complaint record was silently dropped before the call was made.

items.question: A publishing house's manuscript-assessment service sends whole manuscripts of 40 to 80 MB through the company's central model gateway. The gateway now dominates memory usage in its cluster, its audit store is growing far faster than forecast, and p99 gateway latency has degraded for the six other teams that share it. What should the architect change?

options.A: Grant the manuscript service a direct path to the provider that bypasses the gateway, since its payload profile is unlike everyone else's.
options.B: Increase the gateway's memory limits and expand the audit store's capacity so the manuscript workload fits comfortably alongside the other six teams.
options.C: Have the application extract the relevant sections before the call, and have the gateway audit a digest and a reference, not the body.
options.D: Compress request bodies in transit so that both the gateway's memory footprint and the audit store's growth rate are meaningfully reduced.

items.question: A dental care network's appointment-recall pipeline consumes about five events per second. A defective prompt-template deployment made the model worker throw on every message for five hours, and roughly 90,000 events are now in the dead-letter queue. The template has been rolled back and the workers are healthy. Each successfully processed event sends an SMS to a patient. The team proposes replaying the dead-letter queue immediately. What should the engineer do next?

options.A: Replay a bounded sample through the normal idempotent path, confirm no duplicate patient messages appear, then drain the rest at a throttled rate.
options.B: Replay all 90,000 messages now through the normal consumer path, since the template defect is fixed and the events have already waited more than five hours.
options.C: Raise consumer concurrency substantially so the 90,000-message backlog clears quickly and the pipeline returns to real-time processing.
options.D: Purge the dead-letter queue and rely on the next scheduled recall run to pick up the affected patients on its normal weekly cycle.

items.question: A treasury team asks for a Claude feature that computes statutory late-payment interest from a published formula, an invoice amount and a payment date. Why does this fail use-case qualification as an LLM problem?

options.A: Financial calculations performed by a language model are prohibited under standard external audit rules.
options.B: Interest figures cannot be returned reliably in a structured response field, so every result would need re-keying by hand.
options.C: Claude cannot apply a formula supplied in a system prompt without first being fine-tuned on worked examples.
options.D: A fixed rule already yields one verifiable answer, so deterministic code is cheaper, exact and trivially auditable.

items.question: A logistics operator's VP of Operations describes delayed-shipment exception handling as a three-rule process and asks for it to be automated. Before design, the architect samples 60 recent exceptions from the case system: 24 of them were resolved by a dispatcher phoning the carrier and applying a judgement that appears nowhere in the three rules, and those 24 account for roughly two-thirds of total handling minutes. What should discovery do next?

options.A: Sit with the dispatchers who resolved those 24 cases, reconstruct what they decided and on what basis, and treat that as the requirement.
options.B: Ask the VP to arbitrate at the next operations review and issue new written policy covering the missing situations before design begins.
options.C: Build to the three documented rules and log the remaining 24 cases as out-of-scope exceptions for the pilot, without further inquiry.
options.D: Report requirements as unstable and hold discovery until Operations publishes a complete written procedure covering the phone-call exceptions.

items.question: A health insurer is piloting Claude-assisted triage of prior-authorisation requests and intends to claim a reduction in turnaround time. The same programme is also replacing the clinician intake form and re-routing three work queues, and the current plan lands all three changes on pilot go-live day. Warehouse history is retained indefinitely. What must discovery secure now?

options.A: Adopt the industry benchmark for triage-time reduction published by the workflow vendor in its annual utilisation study as the comparison point.
options.B: Defer measurement until the pilot has run thirty days, so the comparison window matches the post-change period in length and case mix.
options.C: Reconstruct the baseline from warehouse history after go-live, since the pre-change records are preserved and can be queried at any time.
options.D: Measure turnaround, rework rate and cost per case now, and sequence the intake-form and routing changes away from pilot go-live.

items.question: A publisher wants Claude to score pitched article ideas for likely audience performance so editors can prioritise commissioning. Six years of history is available: every published article has full traffic data, but pitches that editors rejected were never written and have no outcome recorded. The sponsor wants an accuracy acceptance criterion agreed this week. What is the most important thing to establish in discovery?

options.A: This is a numeric prediction task, so a gradient-boosted regressor over article metadata — section, author, length, season — fits better than a language model.
options.B: The use case is feasible as it stands; run a model-graded scoring pass over historical pitches and calibrate the scores to traffic deciles.
options.C: Six years is too short a history; predictive audience models conventionally need a decade of traffic outcomes to stabilise seasonal effects.
options.D: Outcome data exists only for approved pitches, so a target measured on that history says nothing about the rejected population the tool re-ranks.

items.question: A discovery workshop produces the requirement 'the assistant must be accurate'. Which set of elements is the minimum needed to turn that into an acceptance criterion the team can pass or fail?

options.A: A self-reported confidence-score cut-off, a fixed sampling temperature and a retry-on-failure policy.
options.B: A sponsor signature on the design document, an agreed go-live date and a documented rollback plan.
options.C: A defined metric, a numeric threshold, a frozen evaluation set, and the grader that scores it.
options.D: A chosen model tier, a version-controlled prompt template and a p95 latency budget for the call.

items.question: A water utility wants Claude to read scanned field-inspection reports — pre-printed forms with handwritten annotations, photographed by engineers on tablets — and populate an asset-defect register. The architect has two weeks before a funding decision. Which TWO activities produce the most decision-relevant evidence in that window? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Build the ingestion pipeline that moves scans from the document store into object storage, ready for batch processing.
options.B: Have a person extract the target fields from fifty sampled scans, recording how often a field is illegible or absent.
options.C: Assemble a labelled corpus of five thousand reports so a fine-tune can be scheduled if prompting underperforms on tablet photos.
options.D: Run Claude over the same fifty sampled scans and score its field-level output against the hand-made human key.
options.E: Produce the deployment comparison between the first-party API and a cloud-provider-hosted deployment of the model.

items.question: A housing authority is six weeks into a ten-week discovery for a Claude assistant that drafts replies to tenant repair queries. The data protection officer confirms the maintenance case history contains free-text notes with third-party personal data, so access requires a completed impact assessment — realistically eight weeks. A query-volume audit taken during discovery shows 55% of tenant queries are pure status questions answerable from structured repair-status fields, which are already approved for use. The sponsor wants a signed-off design in four weeks. What is the best next step?

options.A: Scope the near-term deliverable to status queries served by the already-approved structured fields, with the assessment as the phase-two gate.
options.B: Ask the sponsor to authorise a time-limited exception to the impact-assessment requirement so the design can be signed off on the agreed date.
options.C: Continue the design against synthetic case notes generated to resemble the real ones, and validate against production data once the assessment clears.
options.D: Suspend the engagement, stand the discovery team down, and re-plan the whole programme once the impact assessment has completed.

items.question: A retailer must ship a returns-eligibility assistant seven weeks before peak trading. Discovery has inventoried nine return reasons. Two of them, 'faulty' and 'changed mind', are 78% of volume and are governed by crisp published policy rules. Of the remaining seven, warranty claims require reading individual supplier contracts and a legal sign-off that has not started. The stated value hypothesis is deflecting routine returns contacts from the call centre. Which de-scoping decision is right?

options.A: Ship all nine return reasons and lower the accuracy acceptance threshold so the long-tail reasons can clear the gate before peak.
options.B: Ship the seven low-volume reasons first, because those are the ones agents find hardest and where assistance is most valuable per case.
options.C: Ship the two high-volume reasons, 'faulty' and 'changed mind', with a deterministic hand-off to a call-centre agent for everything else.
options.D: Ship a general assistant that answers from the published returns policy page for all nine reasons and defer per-reason eligibility logic entirely.

items.question: A programme defines a single success criterion: 'reduce cost per claim by 12% over the coming fiscal year.' Why is a lagging business outcome insufficient on its own as the success definition?

options.A: Cost per claim is owned by the finance function's reporting line and cannot be adopted as a criterion by a technical programme.
options.B: Lagging outcomes cannot be computed from a frozen evaluation set, which disqualifies them as acceptance criteria of any kind.
options.C: Percentage targets are inherently unfalsifiable, because the denominator can be redefined at reporting time by restating claim volume.
options.D: Confounded by outside factors and arriving too late to steer the build, it must be paired with leading measures the team reads weekly.

items.question: A legal services firm plans to use Claude to classify inbound contracts into fourteen risk categories for triage. Before building, the architect has five senior paralegals independently label the same 200 contracts. They agree unanimously on 61%, a majority agrees on a further 27%, and on the remaining 12% there is no majority at all. What is the most important implication for the acceptance criteria?

options.A: Five raters is too small a panel; expand to fifteen paralegals, recompute the agreement statistic and only then discuss a target.
options.B: Score acceptance on an adjudicated gold set with a written tie-break rule, and make the no-majority cases a routing class, not errors.
options.C: Set the acceptance target at 88% accuracy, matching the combined unanimous and majority agreement rate of the paralegal panel.
options.D: Disagreement at this level shows the fourteen-category taxonomy is not automatable, and the use case should be declined at the triage gate.

items.question: A German manufacturing subsidiary wants Claude to summarise shift-handover notes and flag safety concerns. The design surfaces recurring patterns attributable to individual operators. The plant director is the sponsor and has budget. Which stakeholder must be mapped and engaged during discovery, before the design is committed?

options.A: The works council, since per-operator signals engage statutory co-determination and it can withhold agreement after the build.
options.B: The corporate communications team, who own the press release and how the initiative is described to customers.
options.C: The vector database vendor's account team, who will size the embedding index and quote the storage tier for six years of handover notes.
options.D: The finance business partner, who signs off the cloud and licence budget once the design has been fully costed.

items.question: In a pharmacovigilance discovery session, the safety officer states that a system extracting adverse-event details from case narratives 'must never miss an event'. The unit receives about 3,000 narratives a month and eleven trained reviewers currently read every one of them; that will not change. How should the architect convert this into requirements?

options.A: Set a precision target instead, since spurious event reports filed to the regulator are what create exposure in this domain.
options.B: Accept 100% recall as a hard acceptance gate and hold go-live until an evaluation on a held-out narrative set demonstrates it.
options.C: Set a recall target for detection with review retained on every narrative, and measure value in reviewer minutes per case, not cases removed.
options.D: Replace extraction with a deterministic keyword search over the narratives against the MedDRA preferred-term list, so behaviour is fully auditable.

items.question: A telecommunications group's AI council triages roughly forty candidate use cases each quarter. Which THREE findings should disqualify a candidate at the triage gate, rather than being admitted to design as a managed risk? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: There is no way, even in hindsight and with the full case file, to determine whether a given output was correct.
options.B: The source data sits in a mainframe with no API, so a nightly batch extract into the group data lake would have to be built.
options.C: No named business owner has been identified as accountable for the outcome metric the candidate claims to move.
options.D: The current process has never been measured, so no baseline for handling time or cost exists today.
options.E: The output is an exact figure fixed by a regulator's published formula and must be reproducible on demand.

items.question: An insurer receives a particular notification form from brokers. About 90% arrive as machine-generated PDFs from four broker systems whose layouts have been byte-stable for six years; the remaining 10% are scans of handwritten forms from small brokerages. The product owner asks for 'Claude to read all of them'. What should discovery recommend?

options.A: Decline the use case; extraction across mixed print-and-handwriting input quality is not a viable application pattern.
options.B: Use the model on the four machine-generated layouts, and template-based OCR with field-position rules on the handwritten scans.
options.C: Use the model on all inbound notifications, so there is a single code path to maintain and no template-drift exposure when brokers change systems.
options.D: Parse the four known layouts deterministically with a validation check on the fields, sending handwritten scans and validation failures to the model.

items.question: In a discovery workshop at an energy retailer on billing-dispute handling, two senior agents give contradictory accounts of goodwill credits: one says any agent may authorise up to £50, the other says anything above £20 needs a team-leader code. Both believe they are following current policy. The billing system records the amount and the authorising user id for every credit issued. Forty minutes of the session remain. What is the best next step?

options.A: Adopt the more conservative account — £20 with a team-leader code — as the requirement, since the safer threshold cannot cause an overpayment.
options.B: Query recent authorised credits, read the real threshold and approver pattern off the records, and put that rule to the policy owner.
options.C: Log both accounts as a requirements conflict and escalate to the billing policy owner for a written ruling before the workshop proceeds.
options.D: Facilitate the two agents to consensus in the remaining forty minutes and record the threshold they agree on as the requirement.

items.question: A payments processor is scoping automated merchant onboarding. The decision call sits inside a checkout provider's API contract with a 400ms p99 budget for the entire call, and breaching it triggers contractual penalties. The proposal is that Claude fetch the merchant's website, its filings and adverse-media results, reason over them, and return a risk narrative and score inside that call. What is the correct discovery conclusion?

options.A: Feasible if the website, filings and adverse-media results are fetched in parallel and the model's response is streamed to the caller.
options.B: Not feasible at all; merchant risk assessment cannot be automated with a language model and must remain a manual underwriter review.
options.C: The narrative step cannot fit the budget; compute merchant risk asynchronously before onboarding so the synchronous call reads a stored verdict.
options.D: Feasible if the smallest model tier is used, extended thinking is left off, and prompt caching is applied to the system prompt and policy text.

items.question: A grocery chain's supplier-invoice query desk is the target of a Claude assistant, and the business case commits to a 30% reduction in the cost of running the desk. Which TWO measurements must be taken on the current process before the build starts for that specific claim to be testable afterwards? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The average token count of a supplier email thread, for sizing the context window and the per-call spend.
options.B: Fully-loaded cost per resolved query today, including the rate at which resolved queries are re-opened.
options.C: The desk's staff engagement score from the annual colleague survey, tracked as a change-management indicator.
options.D: Estimated per-query API cost, derived from running a prompt prototype over a handful of sample queries.
options.E: The volume distribution of query types, so the share of demand the assistant can address is known.

items.question: In requirement elicitation, why do experienced architects ask a business team for twenty recent real work items with their outcomes rather than for a description of how the work is done?

options.A: Descriptions give the intended process and omit the exceptions driving most of the effort; real items expose them and seed the eval set.
options.B: Real items with outcomes are needed as training pairs for a fine-tune, which a written process description cannot supply.
options.C: Written descriptions cannot be held in the requirements repository in a traceable form that model-risk auditors will accept at review.
options.D: Working from real items lets the team skip the separate baseline measurement of the current process entirely.

items.question: Discovery teams reliably map the sponsor, the budget holder and the end users. Which group is most often left out, and whose omission most often shows up later as failed adoption?

options.A: The infrastructure team who provision the runtime environment and the network route to the model endpoint.
options.B: People whose work the system changes without their using it — reviewers and second-line teams who absorb its output.
options.C: The internal communications team who will announce the launch on the staff intranet and in the weekly team briefings.
options.D: The model provider's customer success contact, who runs the quarterly service review and the usage report.

items.question: A specialty food distributor asks for Claude to predict next month's order volume for each of 12,000 SKU-and-depot combinations, using four years of transaction history, a promotions calendar, and free-text supplier and account-manager notes. What should discovery conclude?

options.A: Feasible as asked: place the last twenty-four months of history for each SKU-and-depot combination in the prompt and ask for a numeric forecast.
options.B: Feasible if the transaction history is indexed for retrieval so each forecast call sees only the relevant SKU-and-depot series and its promotions.
options.C: The numeric forecast belongs to a statistical forecaster; the model's work is turning the free-text notes into features and explaining variances.
options.D: Feasible only if a model is fine-tuned on the four years of transaction history so that seasonality and promotion lift are learned into the weights.

items.question: A telecommunications provider proposes a single acceptance criterion for its chat assistant pilot: containment rate of at least 60%, where containment means the chat ended without transfer to a human agent. Discovery finds that 18% of today's chats are outage reports needing a field visit the assistant cannot book, and that in 200 transcripts from a vendor demo deployment, 31% of contained chats were followed by the same customer contacting again within 48 hours. What is the most serious defect in this as the sole acceptance criterion?

options.A: Sixty percent is unrealistic for a first pilot and should be reset to the level comparable operator deployments achieve in their first year.
options.B: Containment cannot be computed automatically from the chat platform and would need manual review of every transcript, making the criterion impractical.
options.C: Containment should be reported per intent so the 18% of outage chats can be removed from the denominator before the 60% target is applied.
options.D: Containment counts the absence of a transfer, not whether the problem was solved; it must be paired with a repeat-contact resolution measure.

items.question: A wealth management firm wants Claude to draft annual client review letters. The head of client experience insists the letters must 'sound like us' but cannot state any rule, and rejects sample drafts on instinct. Which TWO elicitation moves are most likely to yield a specifiable requirement? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Collect twenty letters she considers exemplary and ten she rejects, and have her mark the passages that drove each judgement.
options.B: Ask her to complete the brand team's tone questionnaire, scoring the desired voice on twenty adjective scales from formal to warm.
options.C: Derive a style guide from the firm's public marketing website and prospectus, and ask her to approve it as the drafting standard.
options.D: Produce three deliberately different drafts of the same real client letter and have her choose between them and annotate why.
options.E: Defer tone to a post-launch adviser feedback loop, on the basis that a subjective voice cannot be specified in advance.

items.question: A regional airline's crew planning team asks for Claude to check crew duty-time legality. A deterministic rules engine performs this today and has produced no legality breach in three years of operation. The team's stated frustration is that when the engine rejects a roster, its coded messages are unintelligible to crew and planners, generating around 40 support calls a week. What should qualification conclude?

options.A: Re-target at the real pain — turning rejection codes and the relevant rule text into plain language — and leave legality with the engine.
options.B: Have the model re-check every roster the engine passes, running in parallel as an independent second opinion on duty-time legality.
options.C: Replace the rules engine so a single system both determines duty-time legality and explains its reasoning in natural language.
options.D: Decline the request; generating explanations is presentational polish and does not justify funding a delivery programme.

items.question: Discovery produces a short problem statement for each qualified use case. Which set of elements makes that statement usable as the basis for both design and acceptance?

options.A: The competitive landscape, the vendor shortlist and the procurement route through the group framework agreement.
options.B: The sponsor's name, the cost-centre budget code and the target go-live quarter in the portfolio plan.
options.C: Who decides today, which inputs they use, what output they produce, how often, and the cost of getting it wrong.
options.D: The chosen model tier, the integration pattern and the estimated monthly run cost at forecast call volume.

items.question: A pharmaceutical distributor wants Claude to answer field representatives' product availability questions from the ERP. During discovery the architect runs 80 real questions directly against the ERP: in 34 of them the ERP stock figure differs from the warehouse's own physical count by more than 10%. The reconciliation gap is known internally and has no owner. The sponsor wants a working prototype in three weeks. What is the best next step?

options.A: Build the prototype on the ERP stock figures and attach a standing disclaimer to every answer that availability is indicative rather than guaranteed.
options.B: Take the finding to the sponsor as a precondition: either the reconciliation gap gets an owner and a remediation date, or availability drops out of scope.
options.C: Add retrieval over the warehouse physical-count system so the assistant reconciles the two figures at answer time and reports any discrepancy to the rep.
options.D: Lower the accuracy acceptance threshold for availability answers so that it sits under the known ERP data-quality ceiling and the gate can be cleared.

items.question: A property management company wants an assistant that answers tenant queries and can also cancel or reschedule contractor appointments in the scheduling system. Discovery establishes that a cancellation is irreversible in that system: the slot returns to the contractor's open pool and is often taken within minutes, and cancellations inside 24 hours also incur a contractor fee. The sponsor wants both capabilities in phase one. What scope should discovery recommend?

options.A: Include both, with a confirmation question quoting the appointment date to the tenant before any cancellation is executed.
options.B: Include both, but permit write actions only on appointments more than 24 hours away, where no contractor fee applies.
options.C: Include both, and log every write action with its triggering transcript so mistakes can be identified and put right the next day.
options.D: Ship read-only in phase one and gate write actions on phase-one evidence that the assistant reads reschedule intent correctly.
